<reason>A (CON) won the debate's central clash: who reaches the person who never crosses a threshold. A's pressure questions extracted the debate's key concessions — B admitted hours "don't teleport the never-visitor" and could only locate the homebound woman through referral/check-in functions, which A convincingly absorbed as the app-coordinated finding layer ("Fund the list"). A also answered B's pressure more cleanly: the opt-in problem was solved with volunteer-side software fed by daughters, mail carriers, and paramedics, and A correctly noted the motion says invest "more," not close buildings, defusing B's "rooms go dark" framing. A's inversion of B's "near zero" concession into a marginal-dollar argument, the measurability point ("a deleted app leaves a name; the never-visitor leaves nothing"), and the closing flip of B's own final line ("the doorbell takes care of itself" — Chicago shows it doesn't) gave A the cleaner path. B's best live routes — the mobile lonely needing somewhere open at 11pm and the destination/scaffolding frame — were genuinely strong and well-phrased but left the never-member detection gap unresolved. A's clipped Rebuttal 1 is a minor execution cost, not enough to offset the substantive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2: after B honestly conceded hours cannot reach never-visitors and answered "which listed item finds her?" with homebound delivery, check-ins, and referrals, A cataloged the surrender — "Sensors only sense members," and B's answer is itself an outreach list, i.e., the app mechanism — converting B's own answers into the CON case. A's closing then weaponized B's final line as the exact assumption that killed Chicago's isolated seniors.</best_rebuttal>
